items.title: A bounded linear functional on $L^p(\mu)$ and its operator norm
items.strategy: Record the concrete notion: a linear map $\Lambda:L^p(\mu)\to\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ is bounded when $|\Lambda f|\le C\|f\|_p$ for some finite $C$, and define its norm as the supremum over the $L^p$ unit ball. This keeps MT-16 out of dual-space vocabulary while still naming the load-bearing bound.

items.title: Every $g\in L^q(\mu)$ defines a bounded linear functional on $L^p(\mu)$
items.strategy: Use Holder to show $\int fg$ is absolutely convergent and independent of representatives. The map $[f]\mapsto\int fg\,d\mu$ is then linear and bounded on the quotient.

items.title: The functional $\Lambda_g$ has norm $\|g\|_q$; for $q=\infty$ assume $\mu$ is semifinite
items.strategy: The upper bound is Holder. For $1<p<\infty$, choose a real-valued representative $u$ of $g$ and test against the normalized function $|u|^{q-1}\operatorname{sgn}u$. For $p=1$ and $q=\infty$, first isolate the zero class, then use semifiniteness to choose a positive finite-measure subset of an almost-maximal level set of $|u|$.

items.title: On a semifinite measure space, a representing $L^q$ function is unique
items.strategy: If $\Lambda_g=\Lambda_h$, then $\Lambda_{g-h}=0$. The previous norm formula forces $\|g-h\|_q=0$, so the representing function is unique in $L^q$ whenever the $q=\infty$ endpoint is legitimate, namely on a semifinite measure space.

items.title: For $1 \le p < \infty$, every $L^p(\mu)$ class has a sigma-finite essential support
items.strategy: Choose a measurable representative $u$. For each $n$, the level set $\{|u|\ge 1/n\}$ has finite measure by Chebyshev-Markov applied to $|u|^p$, and their union is the essential support of $u$.

items.title: On a finite-measure space, a bounded functional on $L^p$ defines a finite signed or complex measure
items.strategy: On a finite-measure space every indicator $\mathbf 1_E$ lies in $L^p$. Define $\nu(E)=\Lambda(\mathbf 1_E)$ and prove countable additivity from continuity of $\Lambda$ and the $L^p$ convergence of partial indicator sums.

items.title: The measure defined by a bounded $L^p$ functional is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$
items.strategy: If $\mu(E)=0$, then $\mathbf 1_E$ is the zero class in $L^p$, so the induced measure from the previous lemma vanishes on $E$. That is the exact absolute-continuity input needed for Radon-Nikodym.

items.title: On a finite-measure space, a bounded $L^p$ functional is integration against its Radon-Nikodym density
items.strategy: Apply the signed or complex Radon-Nikodym theorem to the induced measure from the previous two lemmas. First identify $\Lambda$ with integration against the resulting density on indicators and simple functions, then extend to all of $L^p$ by MT-15 density.

items.title: The Radon-Nikodym density of a bounded $L^p$ functional belongs to $L^q$
items.strategy: Use the previous representation on finite-measure spaces and then test the density against truncated extremizers. For $1<q<\infty$ this reproduces the usual $|g_k|^{q-1}$ argument; for $q=\infty$ it bounds the essential supremum by the operator norm.

items.title: On a sigma-finite measure space, every bounded linear functional on $L^p$ is integration against a unique $L^q$ function
items.strategy: Choose a sigma-finite exhaustion $X_n$. The finite-measure lemmas produce compatible local densities $g_n$; uniqueness on overlaps lets them glue, and monotone or dominated convergence passes the local formula and the norm bound to all of $L^p$.

items.title: For $1 < p < \infty$, the same representation theorem holds on arbitrary measure spaces
items.strategy: For each sigma-finite measurable $E$, apply the previous theorem to the restricted functional. Under Countable Choice, select countably many near-maximizing sets and witnessing finite-measure exhaustions, take their sigma-finite union, zero-extend its density to $X$, and use the sigma-finite-support lemma to capture every $L^p$ test function.

items.title: The $L^p$ norm is the supremum of pairings against unit $L^q$ functions
items.strategy: Combine the easy direction with the representation theorem: Holder gives the upper bound, while the duality theorem supplies a norm-one representing function for the lower bound. The $p=1$ endpoint is kept at the same sigma-finite hypothesis as the preceding theorem.

items.title: Counting measure specializes the representation theorem to $\ell^p$ and $\ell^q$
items.strategy: Counting measure on $\mathbb N$ is sigma-finite, and $\ell^p$ is already identified with $L^p$ of counting measure. Apply the sigma-finite theorem there to recover the usual sequence-space duality concretely.

items.title: The $p=\infty$ case is recorded but not proved here
items.strategy: Keep the boundary honest: the natural map from $L^1$ into bounded functionals on $L^\infty$ is not onto, but the page does not construct a witness because every standard construction uses Hahn-Banach. Cite the published deferred remark instead.

items.title: Orientation only: the dual-space phrasing of the concrete $L^p$ theorem
items.strategy: This is the one orientation-only remark the design allows. It restates the concrete theorem in the language that the later functional-analysis page will own, without changing the hypotheses or re-proving anything.

title: The Duality of $L^p$ and Lq — Examples

items.title: A power function on $(0,1]$ realizes the duality norm on the unit interval
items.strategy: Take $g(x)=x^{-a}$ with $0<a<1/q$, normalize the extremizer $|g|^{q-1}$ explicitly, and compute both norms by one-variable power integrals.

items.title: The functional $f\mapsto\int_0^{1/2} f$ on $L^p[0,1]$ has norm $2^{-1/q}$
items.strategy: Here the representing function is the indicator of $[0,1/2]$. Its $L^q$ norm is $\lambda([0,1/2])^{1/q}=2^{-1/q}$, with the usual $q=\infty$ interpretation at $p=1$, so the functional's norm is read off from the A-page norm theorem.

items.title: Every bounded linear functional on $\ell^2$ is summation against a unique $\ell^2$ sequence
items.strategy: Specialize the counting-measure corollary to $p=q=2$ and spell out the pairing as $a\mapsto\sum_n a_n b_n$. This is the clean concrete Hilbert-space case the design asked for, but stated without invoking abstract Hilbert-space Riesz vocabulary.

items.title: Point evaluation at $0$ is not well defined on $L^p[0,1]$
items.strategy: Change a representative of the zero $L^p$ class at the single point $0$. The two representatives define different evaluation values, so point evaluation does not descend to an $L^p$ class.

items.title: The zero-countable / infinity-cocountable measure space breaks the $p=1$ endpoint of duality
items.strategy: Build the countable-cocountable measure directly, then use Chebyshev-Markov to force every $L^1$ representative to vanish off an at most countable set while $L^\infty$ still contains distinct bounded representatives.

items.title: A bounded functional on $L^\infty[0,1]$ need not come from $L^1[0,1]$
items.strategy: Record the Folland-Hunter boundary witness as a citation-only remark: extend point evaluation from $C([0,1])$ to $L^\infty([0,1])$ by Hahn-Banach, and note that no $L^1$ density can produce it. This item is source-cited and proved_here=false at authoring.
